Q: Linking to the correct table in a Foreign Relationship A:

I initially thought that Enrollment should be linked to StudentProfile since logically a student enrolls in a course. However, after reconsidering the design, it makes more sense to associate Enrollment with the User model.

The main reason is that User represents the core identity and is directly tied to authentication and actions in the system. Enrollment is essentially an action performed by a user, so linking it to User keeps the design simpler and more flexible.

This approach also avoids unnecessary joins when querying (e.g., request.user.enrollments.all()), and it allows for easier scalability in case roles evolve (like a user being both a teacher and a student).

The StudentProfile should remain focused on storing additional, role-specific data rather than being responsible for core relationships like enrollments.

So overall, linking Enrollment to User is cleaner, more maintainable, and aligns better with standard Django practices.

Q: Comparing dates in the same column A:

We could use you query as CTE, then we make a self-join to get the expected output:

 with CTE as (
  select 
    item.HeadID as headId,
    item.STARTDate as itemStartDate,
    item.ENDDate as itemEndDate,
  from 
    serv.HEAD head
  inner join 
    serv.ITEM item on item.HeadID = head.HeadID
)
select c.*
from CTE c
inner join CTE t on t.headId = c.headId 
  and ( t.itemStartDate <> c.itemStartDate or t.itemEndDate <> c.itemEndDate)

Q: Pivoting table doesn't return the expected results A:

Try this:

SELECT 
    Attribute_displayname, [Team 1], [Team 2], [Team 3], [Team 4] 
FROM 
    (SELECT Attribute_displayname, Team_name, Value 
     FROM #GenericTeam) AS SRC 
PIVOT 
    (MAX(Value) FOR Team_name IN ([Team 1], [Team 2], [Team 3], [Team 4])) AS PivotTable

In the PIVOT I changed FOR Value to FOR Team_name because you must use the column where the name of team is.

Then I removed the spaces from the team name columns - since they don't currently match the values shown.

Q: How to reduce Google Distance Matrix API cost in a location-based application? A:

To cut down your API costs, I think you definitely shouldn't be sending all 150 locations to Google. You may try just using your $geoNear results to filter down to the top 10 or 15 nearest places using basic straight-line distance first, and only pass that subset to the Distance Matrix API.

Regarding caching distances in Redis to save money, take note that this is a direct violation of the Google Maps Platform Service Specific Terms, which strictly prohibits caching if it prevents them from tracking your usage for billing (1.4 (e)), though they do let you cache Place IDs indefinitely and allow temporary caching just to improve network performance (1.4 (a)). If you were caching strictly for performance and needed to group small coordinate changes, snapping your lat/lng coordinates to about 3 decimal places should work fine to hit the same cache keys.

Due to these restrictive ToS rules, using an alternative like OSRM might be the better route for heavy calculation volumes, but be careful that if you do use Google's Distance Matrix API for any of your logic, you cannot display that data on a non-Google map (2.3).

Q: JAVA/MSSQL: com.microsoft.sqlserver.jdbc.SQLServerException: The connection is closed A:

That can be caused by several reasons:

  1. A bug in your script. The connection is closed somewhere (maybe because of an exception which you don't handle properly) and then you try to use it again. Check exception and resource handling.

  2. You're keeping a connection open for too long. After a certain timeout, the database closes the connection on their side.

  3. Someone restarted the database server.

It's most likely not a firewall issue; firewalls just drop packets when the connection times out, so the application appears to "hang" instead of giving a good error message.

Q: POST request failed with 405 Not Allowed when Spring Security is on A:

I had the exact issue and I think it might relate to your issue as well. one of my @RestControllers didn't have @RequestMapping("/myendpoint") on the class. this alone was causing a 405 method not allowed error for my websocket.

I couldn't figure the reason for this behavior either but "maybe" the absence of @RequestMapping on the controller was causing the requests from websocket ending up on this controller's endpoint, since the controller is only accepting POST requests by default you would get 405 method not allowed.

I believe if you had specified endpoints for your @RequestMappings specially the GET type:

@RequestMapping(value = "/me/myendpoint" , method = RequestMethod.GET)
public LoginDTO getLoginDTO(){
    return new LoginDTO();
}

it would solve your problem.
